title: 71% of Gen Z Say Diwali Is Best Celebrated the Traditional Way, Survey Finds
excerpt: A YouGov India survey of 1,203 respondents aged 18-29, commissioned by Sanrio, finds young Indians holding to Diwali tradition while making it more personal — thoughtful gifts over expensive ones, smaller gatherings, and food as self-expression.
body:
• 71% of Gen Z respondents said Diwali is best celebrated the traditional way, in an online YouGov India survey of 1,203 people aged 18-29 across Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai, conducted October 7-14, 2026.
  • Two-thirds (66%) also want more playfulness in the festival, and 60% would rather celebrate in smaller groups where they can be themselves.
  • Gifting is getting personal: 64% prefer a gift that shows the giver knows their "little habits and quirks" over a more expensive gift, and 60% value personal meaning over impressing on social media.
  • Food is the top channel of self-expression: 72% enjoy personalised festive food, and 43% share or send food to make others feel included.

Young Indians are not walking away from Diwali tradition — they are editing it. In a survey of 1,203 Gen Z respondents conducted online by YouGov India and commissioned by Sanrio, the Japanese company behind Hello Kitty, 71% said the festival is best celebrated the traditional way. At the same time, 66% said they want more playfulness — games and light-hearted moments — woven into it, and 66% said childhood memories strongly shape how they celebrate now.

The survey, released on November 5 ahead of Diwali, covered respondents aged 18 to 29 in Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Chennai, and asked about traditions, gifting, friendship and nostalgia. Its findings describe a generation keeping the rituals and changing the emphasis: smaller, warmer, more personal.

Gifts that prove you know someone

The clearest shift is in gifting. 64% of respondents said they prefer gifts that show the giver understands their "little habits and quirks" over higher-priced gifts. 60% valued a gift with personal meaning understood only by the giver and the recipient over one that impresses on social media, and nearly seven in ten agreed that buying or sending something simply because it reminded them of a friend is a genuine way of showing care. In Bengaluru, 38% said they choose gifts based on the recipient's needs and likes — the highest of the five cities — and 39% said gifts are meaningful when they evoke shared memories.

Smaller circles, fuller plates

Connection, in the survey, comes from time rather than scale. 70% said everyone should feel welcome and included at Diwali, yet 60% would rather celebrate in smaller groups where they can be themselves. Feeling connected came from spending time together (57%), sharing food (49%) and taking photographs and making memories (46%). Food carries unusual weight for this generation: 72% said they enjoy cute, fun or personalised festive food, 54% use food to express their personality, and 43% share or send food to make others feel included — rising to 49% in Chennai.

The cities differed in emphasis. Delhi NCR respondents were the most traditional, with 47% strongly agreeing Diwali is best celebrated the traditional way, against 34% in Hyderabad and 37% in Chennai. In Hyderabad, 68% planned to spend the festival with family, the highest share. In Mumbai, 58% preferred traditional or festive attire over casual wear, and 19% saw celebrations becoming more friendship- and social-focused, against 11-12% in Delhi NCR, Hyderabad and Chennai.

"Seeing Indian Gen Z resonate with Hello Kitty's values of togetherness, friendship and kindness is truly inspiring."

— Ruchi Pangasa, Director, India Operations, Sanrio

Pangasa said young Indians reflecting those principles in how they celebrate Diwali underscored the brand's cultural relevance in India; Sanrio opened its first representative office in Mumbai earlier this year. Because the survey was commissioned by a brand, its numbers are best read as a snapshot of stated attitudes rather than measured behaviour — but the direction is consistent across all five cities: the rituals stay, the guest list shrinks, and the gift has to mean something. For diaspora families raising Gen Z children, that is a recognisable Diwali.
